analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis for Fault-Tolerant Hard Real-Time Tasks with Arbitrary Large Deadlines

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Schedulability analysis based the worst-case response time is an important research issue in realtime systems. Due to the restriction that the traditional schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant real-time systems only considered that the deadline of each task must be no larger than its period, this paper extends the computation model that the deadline of each task can be longer than its period. Based on the worst-case response time schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant hard real-time task set, we present a fault-tolerant priority assignment algorithm for our proposed computation model. This algorithm can be useful, together with schedulability analysis, especially for the real-time communication systems and distribution systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In recent years, computing systems have been used in several applications that have stringent timing constraints, such as autopilot systems and satellite and launch vehicle control. Real-time systems are systems whose correctness depends not only on their logical and functional behavior, but also on the temporal properties of this behavior. In many real-time applications, fault-tolerance is also an important issue. A system is fault-tolerant if it produces correct results even in the presence of faults. Due to the critical nature of tasks supported by many real-time systems, it is essential that tasks complete before their deadlines even in the presence of processor failures. This makes fault-tolerance an inherent requirement of hard realtime systems.

Scheduling theory is one of the major areas of research in real-time systems. Scheduling theory provides policies and mechanisms for ordering the usage of system resources (mainly the processor), and tests to determine the predictability of the system performance. By predictability we mean, whether the system can be proved to be capable of meeting its timing constraints, using worst-case response time estimates. Response time analysis has recently been extended to cope with the possibility of errors in the system's computation [1]. Modeling the recovery of tasks as alternative tasks that should be executed to recover the system from an erroneous state, the authors have shown that fault tolerance based on errorrecovery techniques can be easily modeled by response time analysis. The Real-Time Group of the University of York has always been taking up the schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant real-time systems [1][2][3][4][5]. In [1][2], they use the same fixed-priority assignment algorithms as those used under the fault-free assumption. This approach does not consider appropriate priority assignment schemes to calculate priorities of alternative tasks. Moreover, a new faulttolerant priority assignment policy is proposed in [3,46]. This policy considers the recovery of tasks running with higher priorities. This characteristic is very useful since faulty tasks certainly have a shorter period to meet their deadlines. An extension of this policy is described in [5], which assumed that errors may take place at any time instead of considering that errors take place periodically in worst case. However, the common restriction of the computation model considered in [1][2][3][4][5] is that the deadline must be no greater than the period. Our approach described in this paper removes this requirement of the former computation model. Indeed, here we assume that the deadline can be greater than the period. This extension is particularly useful for

The 2008 International Conference on Embedded Software and Systems (ICESS2008) real-time communication or distributed real-time systems where end-to-end latencies can be quite high compared to the process periods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the assumed computation model. The related work is introduced in Section 3. Then, Section 4 presents our approach to carrying out the schedulability analysis based on the worst-case response time analysis. In Section 5, the method to finding out the optimal fault-tolerant priority configuration is given. At last, Section 6 presents our final comments.

div.head: Computation model
div.p: We assume that there is a set Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 ,…, τ n } of n tasks, called primary tasks that must be scheduled by the system in the absence of faults. Any primary task τ i in Γ has a period T i , a deadline D i and a worst-case computation time C i . Tasks can be periodic or sporadic. For sporadic tasks the period refers to the minimum inter-arrival time. Here, it is important to note that the deadlines are allowed to be arbitrary large, in other words, the deadline D i can be greater than the period T i . It is an extension of the computation model in [3,4].

Each primary task τ i can have a certain number of alternative tasks associated with it. Each alternative task only corresponds to a given action taken to recover τ i from a given fault. Any alternative task has a worst-case computation time. For simplicity we denoted i τ as the alternative task whose worst-case computation time i C is the largest one among these worst-case computation time of all alternative tasks associated with τ i . And we assume that any alternative tasks corresponding to a primary task runs at the same priority level. Thus we only need to refer to i τ as the worst-case alternative task in case of faults in task τ i .
Obviously, i τ has the same deadline as τ i . So the total response time of τ i is the sum of the response time of τ i and that of i τ .

Primary tasks are scheduled according to some fixed priority assignment algorithm (e.g. rate monotonic scheduling algorithm [6] or deadline monotonic scheduling algorithm [7]), which attributes a distinct priority to each primary task. We consider n different priority level (1, 2,…, n), where 1 and n represent the highest and the lowest priority level respectively. We denote p i and i p as the priority of τ i and i τ , respectively. When a primary task, say τ i , and an alternative task, say j τ , are ready to execute at the same priority level, we assume that j τ is scheduled first. Each task τ i may be blocked by lower priority tasks for at most B i units of time as a result of the operation of the Priority Ceiling Protocol [8].

We consider only the occurrence of temporary software faults in a uniprocessor system where recovery techniques such as recovery blocks, exception handling or task re-execution are appropriate. When a fault hits τ i during its execution, the system must schedule the alternative task i τ . We also assume that there is no cost associated with any scheduling of primary or alternative tasks. Also, we assume that all faults are detected by the system and there is no fault propagation, which means that faults affect only the executing task.

We assume in the analysis that there is a minimum time between two consecutive error occurrences, T E . The smaller the value of T E is for which we still meet all deadlines, the stronger the system fault resilience is. Thus, we attribute T E to a standard of the ability to tolerate faults.

div.head: Related work
div.p: Liu and Layland [7] presented an inexact (i.e. sufficient but not necessary) schedulability analysis for period tasks scheduled with fixed priorities when priorities are assigned in rate monotonic order.

The exact formulation of the worst-case response time for fixed priority scheduled tasks was introduced by Joseph and Pandya [9]. Audsley et. al. showed how the response time could be calculated with fix-point iteration [10], thus giving an exact (i.e. both sufficient and necessary) schedulability analysis. Since then worst-case response time analysis has been extended to handle more complex computation models [11], including sporadic tasks, kernel overheads, blocking by low priority tasks, release jitter, arbitrary large deadlines, etc.

In [11], the model used include blocking, release jitter and arbitrary large deadlines are included. When the deadline is allowed to be greater than the period it is possible to invoke a task a second time before the first task invocation has completed execution. This means that the second invocation do not only suffer interference from higher priority tasks, but also suffer interference from the first invocation. Thus, to analyze this model we need to investigate the completion-time for a set of invocations of each task. The completiontime for the k-th invocation, I i,k , (where k = 0 for the first invocation) is given by equation (1).

div.p: For fault-tolerant scheduling, a study done by Burns, Davis and Punnekkat [2] provides schedulability analysis for fault tolerant task sets scheduled with fixed-priority point. Based this work, Lima and Burns [3] studied the approach to run the recovery of tasks with higher priorities and provided an effective schedulability analysis to guarantee the predictability of system with this character. Base on the schedulability analysis, Lima and Burns also provide a method to find out optimal priority configuration, which maximizes the fault resilience of task sets [4]. As far as we know, the scheduling issue of fault tolerant hard real-time task sets with arbitrary large deadlines has never been studied before.

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: In this section we derive schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant hard real-time tasks considering the assumed computation model described in Section 2. Schedulability analysis for real-time tasks is based on the well-known worst-case response time analysis. The traditional response time of task τ i is the time needed to execute τ i and all tasks with each of whose priority is higher than p i . When faults are considered, on the other hand, the time necessary to recovery the fault tasks has to be considered in the calculation of the worst-case response time of task τ i . The basic idea is to compute the worst-case response time of each task in the system, and compare with its deadline. If R i ≤ D i for all tasks, then the system is schedulable, otherwise, the system is unschedulable.

Consider the arbitrary large deadlines. For each task τ i , τ i is invocated for (k+1) times during the completion time of the k-th invocation. Then, the sum of the execution time for itself is given, say (k+1)C i . So the problem to reduce R i divides into two child problems: how to reduce the time for preemption and how to reduce the time for the fault recovery. Note that the computation of the two-section time is related to the running task, which can be some primary tasks or some alternative tasks. As primary tasks are scheduled according to some fixed priority assignment algorithm, the priorities of primary tasks are given. In a sense, the priority assignment algorithm of alternative tasks is a key issue to reduce R i . For fault-tolerant priority assigning, two approaches are proposed in [2] and [4], respectively. One is the fault-tolerant priority inheritance approach [2], and the other is the faulttolerant priority promotion approach [4].

As can be seen from equation ( 3) described in Section 3, the worst-case response time of task τ i with arbitrary large deadline is the difference between the arrival time and completion time in the worst case. Due to the fact that the arrival time for invocation k of task τ i in the worst case is given when the task set Γ is given, the problem to how to reduce R i becomes the problem to how to reduce the completion time for invocation k of task τ i , I i,k . In this section, we mainly discuss the derivation of the completion time for invocation k of task τ i , and derive the worst-case response time of task τ i . In the following sections, we derive the equations of the analysis for the two faulttolerant priority assignment approaches when the deadlines are allowed to be arbitrary large and present some simple but useful properties of the analysis.

div.head: The Optimal Priority Configuration Search Algorithm
div.p: Up to now we have presented the schedulability analysis for the proposed approach, but have not considered the best priority configuration so that the fault resilience of the task set is minimized. In this section, such an optimal priority configuration search algorithm is proposed according to properties of the former worst-case response time analysis.

Before considering the properties of the analysis described earlier, we introduce a function T e (x) [6] . The function means that a given priority configuration, say P x , has a minimum allowed value of T E . If any value less that T e (x) is attributed to T E , some task may be unschedulable. In particular, if T E = T e (x) -1, then there is at least a task τ i in Γ such that R i (x, T e (x)-1) > D i . The tasks that cause the unschedulability of Γ under this circumstance are called dominant tasks, denoted by the task set D(x) formally as D(x) = {τ i ∈Γ|R i (x, T e (x) -1) > D i }.

We assume the response time of task τ i during the m-th invocation of τ i is the worst-case response time of τ i . Let A i,m denote the release (arrival) of the m-th invocation and I i,m (x,T E ) denote the completion time of the m-th invocation. As can be seen from equation ( 2), A i,m is given whichever level the fault-tolerant priority level of task τ i is assigned to. And according to equation ( 6) and ( 9), I i,m (x,T E ) is the function of P x and T E . So we consider the effects to the worst-case response time of the tasks due to two cases, external errors and internal errors, respectively. Firstly, suppose that task τ i is unschedulable due to the external errors. Therefore, the optimal fault-tolerant priority configuration search algorithm regarding the proposed schedulability analysis is described as follows (See Fig. 1). First of all, some initialization is done in lines 1-3. Then, the minimum value for T E regarding the initial priority configuration is calculated in line 4. The initial configuration P x and the found value of T e (x) is saved in variables P x * and T E * , respectively. These values will change throughout the execution of the search algorithm if some optimal priority configuration is found. After the initialization, the optimization procedure is carried out (lines 5-35) until no optimization is possible (line 23 or 30) or T E < L (lines 21).

By the algorithm PCS, P 0 = <0, 0,…,0> is the first saved priority configuration. Assume first that there is no other execution of the block (lines 18-21). This is because the algorithm stops in line 21, 23, or 30, which means that no optimization was possible from P 0 . In other words, for any other priority configuration reached by the algorithm, say P u , the task set is unschedulable with T E = T e (0) -1. As a result, P 0 is optimal. Now, assume that there are at least two (consecutively) saved priority configurations, P v and P x say. By the construction of the algorithm, the values attributed to T E do not increase throughout the iterations. Thus, T e (x) ≤ T e (v). This implies that the last saved priority configuration has the minimum (optimal) value of T E , as required. To this degree, the algorithm PCS finds an optimal configuration priority regarding the proposed analysis.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we firstly extend the computation model of the former scheduability analysis for faulttolerant hard real-time task set. Our assumed computation model allows the deadlines of all tasks to be arbitrary large. Then, a new priority assignment algorithm, which can be used, together with the presented schedulability analysis, to improve system fault resilience as possible as it can. The proposed schedulability analysis takes into account the fact that the deadlines are allowed to be larger than the period. The proposed priority assignment algorithm, which uses some properties of the analysis, is very efficient. The result from the proposed analysis is particularly useful for real-time communication or distributed realtime systems where end-to-end latencies can be quite high compared to the process periods.
